question: What are Python's mutable and immutable data types? Give examples of each.
hinglish_explanation: Dekh bhai, Python mein kuch data types hain jo tu change kar sakta hai creation ke baad (mutable) jaise list, dict, set. Aur kuch hain jo ek baar ban gaye toh change nahi hote (immutable) jaise int, str, tuple. Immutable matlab agar tu value change karega toh naya object banega memory mein.
real_life_example: Soch Aadhaar number - ek baar assign hua toh change nahi hota (immutable). Lekin tera Swiggy cart - items add/remove kar sakta hai freely (mutable). Tuple Aadhaar jaisa hai, list cart jaisi.
how_to_answer: Python mein mutable types hain: list, dict, set - inhe creation ke baad modify kar sakte hain
Immutable types hain: int, float, str, tuple, frozenset - ek baar create hone ke baad change nahi hote
Immutable objects modify karne par naya object banta hai memory mein, purana wahi rehta hai
Yeh important hai kyunki immutable objects hashable hote hain - dictionary keys ke liye use ho sakte hain
Performance wise immutable objects thread-safe hote hain without locks
Example: list append karo toh same object modify hota hai, string concatenate karo toh naya string banta hai

question: Explain the difference between a list and a tuple in Python. When would you use each?
hinglish_explanation: List aur tuple dono sequence hain, lekin list mutable hai (change kar sakte ho) aur tuple immutable (fixed). Tuple fast hota hai aur less memory leta hai. Jab data fix hai toh tuple use karo, jab add/remove karna ho toh list.
real_life_example: Flipkart pe tera order history - tuple jaisi hai, jo hua wo hua change nahi hoga. Lekin tera wishlist - list jaisi hai, aaj kuch add kiya kal kuch remove kiya.
how_to_answer: List mutable hai - append, remove, insert kar sakte hain; Tuple immutable hai - creation ke baad change nahi hota
Tuple list se faster hai iteration mein kyunki fixed size memory allocation hoti hai
Tuple hashable hai toh dictionary key ya set element ban sakta hai, list nahi ban sakta
Tuple use karta hoon jab data fixed ho jaise coordinates (x, y), database row results
List use karta hoon jab dynamic collection chahiye jaise user inputs collect karna
Memory efficiency: tuple less memory consume karta hai compared to same size list
Named tuples use karta hoon lightweight data classes ke liye production mein

question: What is the difference between deep copy and shallow copy in Python?
hinglish_explanation: Shallow copy matlab sirf top-level copy hota hai - nested objects same rehte hain (reference share hota hai). Deep copy matlab poora naya independent object banta hai, nested bhi. Jaise shallow copy mein photocopy mein links same pages pe point karengi, deep copy mein sab kuch naya banega.
real_life_example: Soch tu ek Google Doc share karta hai (shallow copy) - dono log same table edit kar rahe hain. Deep copy matlab tune poora doc duplicate kiya - ab tera changes usko affect nahi karenge. ML mein model config copy karte waqt deep copy use karna padta hai warna original config bhi change ho jaati hai.
how_to_answer: Shallow copy creates new object but nested objects still reference the same memory - import copy; copy.copy()
Deep copy creates completely independent copy including all nested objects - copy.deepcopy()
Assignment operator (=) toh copy bhi nahi karta, bas reference create karta hai
Shallow copy sufficient hai jab flat structures hain (no nested lists/dicts)
Deep copy zaruri hai jab nested mutable objects hain aur independent modification chahiye
Production mein deep copy use karta hoon ML pipeline configs duplicate karte waqt
Performance note: deep copy slower hai kyunki recursively sab copy karta hai

question: What are *args and **kwargs in Python? How do you use them?
hinglish_explanation: Bhai *args matlab tu function mein kitne bhi positional arguments pass kar sakta hai - ye ek tuple ban jaata hai andar. **kwargs matlab kitne bhi keyword arguments (key=value) pass kar sakte ho - ye dict ban jaata hai. Basically flexible functions banane ke liye use hote hain.
real_life_example: Jaise Zomato mein order place karte waqt - main items fix hain (*args jaise pizza, burger) lekin customizations vary karti hain (**kwargs jaise extra_cheese=True, no_onion=True). Function ko pata nahi kitne options aayenge toh kwargs se handle karta hai.
how_to_answer: *args allows passing variable number of positional arguments as a tuple inside the function
**kwargs allows passing variable number of keyword arguments as a dictionary
Order matters in function definition: regular args, *args, keyword args, **kwargs
Use case: wrapper functions, decorators, API endpoint handlers where params vary
In my FastAPI projects, I use **kwargs for passing dynamic config to ML model inference functions
Real example: def train_model(data, *metrics, **hyperparams) - flexible training function
These are essential for writing generic utility functions and decorators in production code

question: Explain list comprehension in Python. How is it different from a regular for loop?
hinglish_explanation: List comprehension ek one-liner hai jo list create karta hai for loop se. Syntax: [expression for item in iterable if condition]. Ye faster hai regular loop se kyunki internally optimized bytecode generate hota hai. Readable bhi hai chhoti transformations ke liye.
real_life_example: Soch tere paas 1000 user reviews hain Flipkart ke. Tujhe sirf 4+ star wale filter karne hain. Regular loop mein 4 lines lagegi, list comprehension mein ek line: good_reviews = [r for r in reviews if r.stars >= 4]. ML mein data preprocessing ke liye bahut use hota hai.
how_to_answer: List comprehension is a concise way to create lists: [expr for x in iterable if condition]
It's faster than regular for loop - approximately 10-30% due to optimized bytecode
Can include conditions (filtering) and nested loops in single expression
I use it heavily in data preprocessing - filtering, transforming features before model training
Dict comprehension and set comprehension bhi hain: {k:v for k,v in items}
Caveat: complex nested comprehensions reduce readability - I keep it to max 2 levels
Generator expression (parentheses instead of brackets) is memory efficient for large datasets

question: What are Python decorators and how do they work?
hinglish_explanation: Decorator ek function hai jo doosre function ko modify karta hai bina uska code change kiye. @ symbol se lagata hai function ke upar. Basically ye function ko wrap kar deta hai - pehle kuch karo, original function call karo, phir kuch aur karo. Logging, timing, authentication ke liye use hota hai.
real_life_example: Jaise security guard building mein (decorator) - tujhe andar jaane se pehle ID check karega (pre-processing), andar jane dega (original function), aur bahar aate waqt log karega (post-processing). FastAPI mein @app.get('/predict') decorator route define karta hai bina boilerplate ke.
how_to_answer: Decorators are functions that modify behavior of other functions without changing their source code
They use closure concept - inner function has access to outer function's variables
Syntax: @decorator above function definition, equivalent to func = decorator(func)
Common use cases: logging, timing, caching, authentication, rate limiting
I use @functools.lru_cache for caching expensive computations in ML pipelines
In FastAPI, decorators define API routes: @app.post('/predict') for model serving endpoints
functools.wraps preserves original function metadata when writing custom decorators

question: What is the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in Python and how does it affect multithreading?
hinglish_explanation: GIL ek mutex lock hai CPython mein jo ensure karta hai ki ek time pe sirf ek thread Python bytecode execute kare. Iska matlab multithreading se CPU-bound tasks faster nahi hote Python mein. I/O bound tasks ke liye threading theek hai, CPU bound ke liye multiprocessing use karo.
real_life_example: Soch ek railway counter hai (GIL) - chahe 10 log line mein ho, ek time pe ek hi insaan ticket le sakta hai. Agar tujhe ML model training parallelize karni hai (CPU-bound), toh multiprocessing use kar - matlab multiple counters khol de. I/O bound (API calls) ke liye threading chalti hai kyunki wait time mein lock release hota hai.
how_to_answer: GIL is a mutex in CPython that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time
It exists to protect CPython's memory management which is not thread-safe
CPU-bound tasks don't benefit from multithreading due to GIL - use multiprocessing instead
I/O-bound tasks (network calls, file reads) benefit from threading because GIL releases during I/O wait
In my ML pipelines, I use multiprocessing for data preprocessing and concurrent.futures for API calls
Alternatives: use NumPy/PyTorch which release GIL in C extensions, or use asyncio for I/O
Python 3.12+ has sub-interpreters and 3.13 has experimental free-threaded mode (no-GIL)

question: Explain the difference between '==' and 'is' operators in Python.
hinglish_explanation: == value comparison karta hai - kya dono ki value same hai? 'is' identity check karta hai - kya dono same memory location pe hain (same object hain)? Integer caching (-5 to 256) ki wajah se chhote numbers ke liye 'is' True aata hai but bade numbers ke liye nahi.
real_life_example: Do log same car model drive karte hain (== True, same value) lekin unke paas alag alag cars hain (is False, different objects). Agar dono literally same car share karte hain toh 'is' True hoga. None check karte waqt hamesha 'is None' use karo, '== None' nahi.
how_to_answer: == checks value equality - whether two objects have the same value
'is' checks identity - whether two references point to the same object in memory
Always use 'is' for None comparison: if x is None, never if x == None
Python caches small integers (-5 to 256) and interned strings, so 'is' may give unexpected True
In production code, == is almost always what you want except for None/True/False/singleton checks
id() function shows memory address - 'is' essentially compares id() of both objects
This distinction matters when dealing with mutable default arguments in functions

question: Explain the difference between @staticmethod and @classmethod in Python. When would you use each?
hinglish_explanation: @staticmethod ko class ya instance ka koi access nahi hota - ye bas ek normal function hai jo class ke andar rakha hai organization ke liye. @classmethod ko cls milta hai (class itself) - ye class level operations ke liye hai jaise factory methods. Instance method ko self milta hai.
real_life_example: Soch ek ModelFactory class hai. @classmethod from_pretrained(cls, name) use karega naya model object banane ke liye (factory pattern). @staticmethod validate_config(config) sirf config check karega - usse class se koi matlab nahi. HuggingFace Transformers mein from_pretrained exactly aise hi kaam karta hai.
how_to_answer: @staticmethod: no access to class or instance, just a utility function namespaced in the class
@classmethod: receives cls as first argument, can access/modify class state, used for factory methods
Instance method: receives self, can access instance attributes and methods
I use @classmethod for alternative constructors: Model.from_config(config_dict)
@staticmethod for pure utility functions: DataProcessor.validate_schema(data)
In ML code, @classmethod is great for loading models from different sources (checkpoint, ONNX, etc.)
Inheritance: @classmethod properly handles subclassing, @staticmethod doesn't

question: What are Python generators and how are they different from regular functions? What is yield?
hinglish_explanation: Generator ek function hai jo yield use karta hai return ki jagah. Ye lazy evaluation karta hai - ek ek item produce karta hai jab zarurat ho, poora list memory mein nahi rakhta. Bade datasets process karte waqt memory bachata hai. next() call karne pe agla item milta hai.
real_life_example: Jaise Netflix shows recommend karta hai - sab 1000 recommendations ek saath load nahi karta, jaise jaise scroll karo waise waise next batch aata hai. ML mein training data batches load karte waqt generator use karta hoon - 10GB data ek saath memory mein nahi daal sakta, batch by batch yield karta hoon.
how_to_answer: Generators use yield instead of return - they pause execution and resume on next() call
They implement lazy evaluation - produce values on demand, not all at once in memory
Memory efficient: processing 10GB file line by line without loading entire file
I use generators for data loading in ML pipelines - yielding batches for training
Generator expressions: (x**2 for x in range(million)) vs list comprehension
They implement iterator protocol (__iter__ and __next__) automatically
Use case in my work: streaming embeddings from large document corpus for FAISS indexing

question: Explain Python's Method Resolution Order (MRO) and how does multiple inheritance work?
hinglish_explanation: Jab ek class multiple classes se inherit karti hai, toh Python ko decide karna padta hai ki method kahan se lena hai. MRO C3 linearization algorithm use karta hai - left to right, depth first, but with consistency. ClassName.mro() se dekh sakte ho order.
real_life_example: Soch ek ML model class hai jo dono DataMixin aur LoggerMixin se inherit karti hai. Dono mein save() method hai. MRO decide karega ki kaunsa save() call hoga. Diamond problem tab aata hai jab dono parents same grandparent se inherit karte hain - Python C3 linearization se solve karta hai.
how_to_answer: MRO determines the order in which base classes are searched for methods - uses C3 linearization
Python supports multiple inheritance unlike Java - a class can inherit from multiple parents
C3 linearization ensures: children before parents, left-to-right order preserved, consistent ordering
super() follows MRO chain, not just immediate parent - enables cooperative multiple inheritance
Check MRO with ClassName.__mro__ or ClassName.mro() method
Diamond problem: when two parents share a grandparent - C3 ensures grandparent called only once
In practice, I use Mixins pattern for adding capabilities like LoggingMixin, CachingMixin to ML pipeline classes

question: What are context managers in Python? Explain the 'with' statement and how to create custom ones.
hinglish_explanation: Context manager resource management ke liye hai - file open karo, kaam karo, automatically close ho jaye chahe error aaye ya na aaye. 'with' statement use karta hai. Custom banane ke liye __enter__ aur __exit__ methods define karo ya @contextmanager decorator use karo.
real_life_example: Jaise hotel room - check-in (__enter__), stay (code block), check-out (__exit__) guaranteed hai chahe tujhe emergency aaye. ML mein database connection, GPU memory allocation, temporary files - sab context managers se handle karta hoon taaki resource leak na ho.
how_to_answer: Context managers handle resource setup and cleanup using __enter__ and __exit__ dunder methods
'with' statement ensures cleanup happens even if exception occurs inside the block
Common uses: file handling, database connections, locks, temporary directories
Two ways to create: class-based (__enter__/__exit__) or @contextlib.contextmanager decorator
In ML work, I use them for: GPU memory management, MLflow run tracking, temp file cleanup
__exit__ receives exception info (type, value, traceback) - can suppress exceptions by returning True
Example: with torch.no_grad(): for inference - context manager disables gradient computation

question: What is monkey patching in Python? What are its risks and when is it useful?
hinglish_explanation: Monkey patching matlab runtime pe kisi class ya module ka method/attribute change kar dena without modifying source code. Testing mein bahut useful hai (mock karna), lekin production mein risky hai kyunki unexpected behavior aa sakta hai aur debugging mushkil ho jaati hai.
real_life_example: Soch tere ML pipeline mein external API call hai. Testing mein tu actual API call nahi karna chahta (cost + slow). Toh tu us function ko monkey patch karke fake response return karwa deta hai. unittest.mock.patch exactly yahi karta hai internally.
how_to_answer: Monkey patching means modifying classes/modules at runtime without changing source code
Common use: replacing methods for testing - mocking external API calls, database queries
unittest.mock.patch is a structured way to monkey patch for testing
Risks: hard to debug, breaks encapsulation, version upgrades can break patches silently
I use it in testing ML pipelines - patching model.predict() to return fixed output for unit tests
In production, avoid monkey patching - use dependency injection or strategy pattern instead
Libraries like gevent monkey-patch socket module for async I/O - acceptable at framework level

question: Explain Python's dunder (magic) methods. Give examples of commonly used ones.
hinglish_explanation: Dunder methods (double underscore) Python ka special protocol hai - __init__, __str__, __len__ etc. Ye define karte hain ki tera object operators aur built-in functions ke saath kaise behave karega. Jaise __add__ define karega toh + operator kaam karega tere objects pe.
real_life_example: Soch tere paas EmbeddingVector class hai. __add__ define kiya toh do vectors ko + se add kar sakta hai. __len__ define kiya toh len(vector) dimension return karega. __repr__ se debugging mein readable output milega. Pandas DataFrame mein __getitem__ ki wajah se df['column'] kaam karta hai.
how_to_answer: __init__: constructor, __del__: destructor, __repr__: developer-friendly string, __str__: user-friendly string
__len__, __getitem__, __setitem__: make objects behave like containers/sequences
__add__, __mul__, __eq__, __lt__: operator overloading for custom objects
__enter__, __exit__: context manager protocol for with statement
__iter__, __next__: iterator protocol for for-loop support
__call__: makes object callable like a function - useful for ML model inference classes
In my work, I use __call__ in PyTorch modules and __getitem__ in custom Dataset classes

question: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism in Python? How do you achieve each?
hinglish_explanation: Concurrency matlab multiple tasks progress kar rahe hain (interleaved, ek time pe ek). Parallelism matlab literally simultaneously execute ho rahe hain (multiple CPUs pe). Python mein threading/asyncio concurrency deta hai, multiprocessing parallelism deta hai. GIL ki wajah se ye distinction important hai.
real_life_example: Concurrency: ek chef 3 dishes bana raha hai - ek pe masala daal ke chhodta hai, dusri stir karta hai, teesri check karta hai. Parallelism: 3 chefs 3 dishes simultaneously bana rahe hain. ML mein - multiple API calls concurrent (asyncio), data preprocessing parallel (multiprocessing).
how_to_answer: Concurrency: multiple tasks making progress (may not run simultaneously) - asyncio, threading
Parallelism: multiple tasks running literally at the same time on different CPU cores - multiprocessing
GIL limits true parallelism in Python threads for CPU-bound work
asyncio: best for I/O-bound with many connections (API calls, web scraping) - single thread, event loop
threading: good for I/O-bound with simpler code, GIL releases during I/O operations
multiprocessing: true parallelism for CPU-bound (data preprocessing, model training on CPU)
In my pipelines: asyncio for batch embedding API calls, multiprocessing for PDF parsing

question: How does Python's garbage collection work? Explain reference counting and cycle detection.
hinglish_explanation: Python primarily reference counting use karta hai - har object ke paas count hai kitne references point kar rahe hain. Zero hone pe delete. Lekin circular references (A->B->A) mein count kabhi zero nahi hota, toh generational garbage collector detect karke clean karta hai.
real_life_example: Reference counting: jaise library book - jab tak kisi ne issue kari hai (reference hai) tab tak shelf pe nahi jayegi. Circular reference: do friends ne ek dusre ko emergency contact likha - dono ka reference hai but actually koi use nahi kar raha. GC detect karega ki ye isolated cycle hai.
how_to_answer: Primary mechanism: reference counting - each object tracks how many references point to it
When reference count hits 0, memory is immediately freed - deterministic and efficient
Problem: circular references (A references B, B references A) - counts never reach 0
Generational GC handles cycles: 3 generations (0, 1, 2) - newer objects collected more frequently
gc module: gc.collect() forces collection, gc.disable() for performance-critical sections
weakref module: create references that don't increment count - useful for caches
In ML: large tensor objects and circular model references can cause memory issues - I use del and gc.collect() after inference

question: Explain Python's descriptor protocol. How do properties, classmethod, and staticmethod work internally?
hinglish_explanation: Descriptors Python ka powerful protocol hai jo attribute access customize karta hai. Koi bhi object jo __get__, __set__, ya __delete__ define kare wo descriptor hai. property() internally descriptor hai. Jab tu obj.x access karta hai, Python descriptor protocol follow karta hai.
real_life_example: Soch ek ML model class hai jisme learning_rate property hai. Tu chahta hai ki 0 se 1 ke beech hi ho. Descriptor use karke validate kar sakta hai - jab bhi koi set kare, automatically check ho. SQLAlchemy columns bhi descriptors hain - Column(Integer) define karta hai ki attribute kaise behave karega.
how_to_answer: Descriptor protocol: any object defining __get__, __set__, or __delete__ is a descriptor
Data descriptor: defines __set__ or __delete__ - takes priority over instance __dict__
Non-data descriptor: only defines __get__ - instance __dict__ takes priority over it
property() is implemented as a data descriptor internally
classmethod and staticmethod are non-data descriptors that customize __get__
Lookup order: data descriptors > instance __dict__ > non-data descriptors > class __dict__
I use custom descriptors for validated model hyperparameters and typed configuration objects

question: How does Python's asyncio event loop work internally? Explain coroutines, tasks, and futures.
hinglish_explanation: asyncio ka event loop ek infinite loop hai jo registered coroutines ko schedule karta hai. Coroutine ek function hai jo await pe pause ho jaata hai. Task coroutine ko wrap karta hai scheduling ke liye. Future ek placeholder hai jo future result represent karta hai. await pe control event loop ko wapas jaata hai.
real_life_example: Event loop ek restaurant manager hai. Coroutines waiters hain. Jab waiter kitchen se order ka wait karta hai (await), manager dusre waiter ko bhejta hai (context switch). Koi thread nahi badla, bas manager efficiently sab handle karta hai. Mere RAG pipeline mein async se 100 embedding API calls simultaneously handle karta hoon.
how_to_answer: Event loop: central scheduler that manages execution of coroutines - runs until all tasks complete
Coroutine: async def function that can be paused (await) and resumed - cooperative multitasking
Task: wraps coroutine for concurrent execution - created via asyncio.create_task()
Future: low-level awaitable representing eventual result of async operation
await yields control back to event loop - lets other coroutines run during I/O wait
asyncio.gather() for running multiple coroutines concurrently - I use for batch API calls
In production: aiohttp for async HTTP, asyncpg for async PostgreSQL in my ML serving pipelines

question: Explain metaclasses in Python. When would you use them vs decorators or __init_subclass__?
hinglish_explanation: Metaclass wo class hai jo classes create karti hai. Jaise class objects ka blueprint hai, metaclass classes ka blueprint hai. type() default metaclass hai. Custom metaclass se tu class creation control kar sakta hai - validation, registration, method injection at class definition time.
real_life_example: Soch ek ML model registry chahiye - jab bhi koi nayi Model subclass define kare, automatically register ho jaye tracking system mein. Metaclass class banate waqt hi register kar degi. Django ORM mein Model metaclass fields ko database columns mein map karti hai at definition time, runtime pe nahi.
how_to_answer: Metaclass is a class whose instances are classes - controls class creation via __new__ and __init__
type is the default metaclass: type(name, bases, namespace) creates a new class
Use __init_subclass__ (Python 3.6+) for simpler cases: hook that runs when subclass is created
Class decorators: modify class after creation - simpler than metaclass for most cases
Metaclass needed when: controlling class dict (OrderedDict), preventing subclassing, abstract enforcement
Preference order: __init_subclass__ > class decorator > metaclass (simplest that works)
Real frameworks using metaclasses: Django ORM models, SQLAlchemy declarative, ABC module

question: How would you profile and optimize a Python application for production? What tools do you use?
hinglish_explanation: Profiling matlab pehle measure karo kahan bottleneck hai, phir optimize karo. cProfile function-level timing deta hai, line_profiler line-by-line, memory_profiler memory usage. Pehle measure, phir optimize - andha optimization mat karo. Production mein APM tools (DataDog, New Relic) use hote hain.
real_life_example: Mere RAG pipeline mein response time 5 seconds tha. cProfile se pata chala 80% time embedding generation mein ja raha hai. Phir batch processing + caching add kiya aur 1.2 seconds pe aa gaya. Bina profiling ke shayad wrong jagah optimize karta.
how_to_answer: cProfile: built-in, function-level CPU profiling - python -m cProfile -s cumulative script.py
line_profiler: line-by-line timing for specific functions - @profile decorator
memory_profiler: track memory usage line by line - essential for large model loading
py-spy: sampling profiler that attaches to running process - no code modification needed
Optimization strategies: caching (lru_cache), vectorization (numpy), async I/O, connection pooling
In ML pipelines: I profile inference latency, batch size optimization, model loading time
Production monitoring: I use MLflow for experiment tracking and custom metrics for latency/throughput

question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING clause in SQL?
hinglish_explanation: WHERE individual rows filter karta hai GROUP BY se pehle. HAVING groups filter karta hai GROUP BY ke baad. WHERE mein aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM) use nahi kar sakte, HAVING mein kar sakte ho. Pehle WHERE filter hota hai, phir grouping, phir HAVING filter.
real_life_example: Swiggy analytics: WHERE clause se sirf Delhi ke orders filter karo (row level). HAVING clause se un restaurants ko dikhao jinke 100 se zyada orders hain (group level). WHERE pehle rows filter karega, phir restaurant-wise group hoga, phir HAVING count check karega.
how_to_answer: WHERE filters individual rows BEFORE grouping - cannot use aggregate functions
HAVING filters groups AFTER GROUP BY - works with aggregate functions like COUNT, SUM, AVG
Execution order: FROM > WHERE > GROUP BY > HAVING > SELECT > ORDER BY
WHERE is more efficient - filters early, reduces data for grouping
Example: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE active=1 GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 100
Use WHERE for column-level filters, HAVING for aggregate-level filters
In my work: WHERE filters relevant documents, HAVING finds categories with enough training data

question: Explain different types of JOINs in SQL with examples.
diagram:
INNER JOIN: A ∩ B (only matching rows)
LEFT JOIN: All A + matching B (NULL where no match)
RIGHT JOIN: All B + matching A (NULL where no match)
FULL OUTER JOIN: All A + All B (NULL where no match on either side)
CROSS JOIN: A × B (cartesian product)
hinglish_explanation: JOIN do ya zyada tables ko combine karta hai. INNER JOIN sirf matching rows deta hai. LEFT JOIN left table ke sab rows + right se matching. RIGHT JOIN ulta. FULL OUTER dono ke sab rows. CROSS JOIN har row ko har row se combine karta hai (cartesian product).
real_life_example: Zomato mein: Users LEFT JOIN Orders - sab users dikhenge chahe unhone order kiya ho ya nahi (inactive users bhi). Users INNER JOIN Orders - sirf wahi users jinke orders hain. Ye analytics mein important hai - kitne users ne kabhi order nahi kiya ye LEFT JOIN se pata chalega (NULL orders).
how_to_answer: INNER JOIN: returns only rows with matching values in both tables - most common and efficient
LEFT JOIN: all rows from left table + matching from right, NULL where no match in right
RIGHT JOIN: all rows from right table + matching from left, NULL where no match in left
FULL OUTER JOIN: all rows from both tables, NULL where no match on either side
CROSS JOIN: cartesian product - every row combined with every other row, rarely used
Performance: INNER JOIN fastest (less data), indexes on JOIN columns critical
In my work: LEFT JOIN user_queries with search_results to analyze queries with no results

question: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL in SQL?
hinglish_explanation: UNION do queries ke results combine karta hai aur duplicates remove karta hai (internally sorting/hashing karta hai). UNION ALL sab rows deta hai including duplicates - faster hai kyunki deduplication nahi karta. Jab duplicates acceptable hain toh UNION ALL use karo performance ke liye.
real_life_example: Flipkart pe search results: ek query title se match karta hai, doosra description se. UNION use karega toh same product ek baar dikhega. UNION ALL mein duplicate aayenge. Jab tujhe count chahiye total matches ka (duplicates count karte hue) toh UNION ALL use kar, unique results ke liye UNION.
how_to_answer: UNION combines results of two SELECT statements and removes duplicate rows
UNION ALL combines results keeping all duplicates - no deduplication step
UNION ALL is significantly faster - avoids sort/hash for deduplication
Both require: same number of columns, compatible data types in corresponding columns
Use UNION ALL by default unless you specifically need deduplication
UNION internally does a DISTINCT operation which adds overhead on large datasets
In my analytics queries: UNION ALL for combining log tables from different months

question: What are indexes in SQL? How do they improve query performance?
hinglish_explanation: Index ek data structure hai (usually B-tree) jo fast lookup allow karta hai bina full table scan ke. Jaise book ki index - poori book padhne ki zarurat nahi, direct page number mil jaata hai. SELECT fast hota hai but INSERT/UPDATE slow ho sakte hain kyunki index bhi update karna padta hai.
real_life_example: Soch Aadhaar database - 130 crore records mein tera Aadhaar number dhundhna hai. Bina index ke har row check karni padegi (table scan). Index se directly mil jaayega O(log n) mein. Lekin har nayi entry pe index update hoga toh INSERT thoda slow hoga.
how_to_answer: Index is a data structure (B-tree, hash) that speeds up data retrieval at cost of storage and write speed
Without index: full table scan O(n), with index: O(log n) for B-tree lookup
Types: B-tree (default, range queries), Hash (equality only), GIN (full-text, arrays), GiST (spatial)
Create on columns used in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY frequently
Trade-off: faster reads but slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE due to index maintenance
Composite index: multiple columns - order matters, leftmost prefix rule applies
In my work: indexed embedding_id and document_id columns in vector search metadata tables

question: Explain window functions in SQL. How are they different from GROUP BY?
hinglish_explanation: Window functions calculations karte hain across a set of rows related to current row - bina rows collapse kiye. GROUP BY rows ko combine karta hai (10 rows -> 1 row per group), window function har row ko rakhta hai aur extra computed column add karta hai. ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG, LEAD etc.
real_life_example: Zomato delivery partner ka monthly ranking chahiye. GROUP BY se sirf total order count milega per partner. Window function se har row mein partner ka rank bhi milega aur individual delivery details bhi preserve rahenge: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY deliveries DESC).
how_to_answer: Window functions perform calculations across a set of rows without collapsing them into groups
Syntax: function() OVER (PARTITION BY col ORDER BY col ROWS BETWEEN...)
Key difference: GROUP BY collapses rows, window functions preserve all rows adding computed columns
Common functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE, LAG, LEAD, SUM, AVG
PARTITION BY is like GROUP BY within window - defines the window frame
Running totals, moving averages, rankings, comparing with previous row - all use window functions
In analytics: I use window functions for computing rolling metrics and user behavior sequences

question: What are CTEs (Common Table Expressions)? How do they compare to subqueries and temp tables?
hinglish_explanation: CTE (WITH clause) ek named temporary result set hai jo query ke scope mein exist karta hai. Readability badhata hai complex queries ki. Subquery se zyada readable hai, temp table se different kyunki ye persist nahi hota. Recursive CTEs hierarchical data traverse karne ke liye use hote hain.
real_life_example: Organization hierarchy - CEO se neeche sab employees ka tree structure nikalna hai. Recursive CTE perfect hai: pehle CEO find karo, phir uske direct reports, phir unke reports... jab tak leaf nodes na aa jaayein. Bina CTE ke ye query nested subqueries ka jungle ban jaati.
how_to_answer: CTE: WITH clause that creates named temporary result set within query scope
Better readability than nested subqueries - can be referenced multiple times in main query
Recursive CTEs: self-referencing for hierarchical/tree data traversal
vs Subquery: CTE more readable, can reference itself, named and reusable within query
vs Temp Table: CTE exists only during query execution, no disk I/O, no explicit cleanup
vs Views: CTE is query-scoped, view is schema-level persistent object
I use CTEs for: multi-step data transformations, recursive category hierarchies, breaking complex analytics

question: Explain ACID properties in database transactions. Why are they important?
hinglish_explanation: ACID ensure karta hai ki database transactions reliable hon. Atomicity: ya toh poora ho ya kuch na ho. Consistency: valid state se valid state mein jaaye. Isolation: concurrent transactions ek dusre ko affect na karein. Durability: commit hone ke baad data persist rahe chahe crash ho.
real_life_example: UPI payment: Atomicity - tere account se 500 kat-te hain AUR dusre mein add hote hain, ya kuch nahi hota (half nahi hoga). Isolation - teri aur kisi aur ki same time payment conflict nahi karegi. Durability - payment successful dikhaya toh crash ke baad bhi data safe hai.
how_to_answer: Atomicity: transaction is all-or-nothing - either all operations succeed or none apply
Consistency: database moves from one valid state to another - constraints maintained
Isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere - appears as if executed sequentially
Durability: once committed, data persists even after system crash - written to disk
Isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE
Trade-off: higher isolation = more consistency but lower concurrency/performance
In my work: ensuring document indexing operations are atomic - either fully indexed or rolled back

question: What is query execution plan? How do you use EXPLAIN to optimize queries?
hinglish_explanation: EXPLAIN command dikhata hai ki database engine query ko kaise execute karega - kaunsa index use hoga, kaunsa join algorithm, kitni rows scan hongi. Ye optimization ka pehla step hai. Seq Scan (bad for large tables), Index Scan (good), Hash Join vs Nested Loop sab yahan dikhta hai.
real_life_example: Jaise Google Maps route suggest karta hai driving ke liye - database bhi query ke liye best 'route' choose karta hai. EXPLAIN ye route dikhata hai. Agar tu dekhta hai Seq Scan on 10M rows toh pata chal gaya index chahiye. Production mein slow queries EXPLAIN se diagnose karta hoon.
how_to_answer: EXPLAIN shows the query execution plan - how database will access data, join tables, sort results
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes and shows real timing + row estimates vs actual
Key things to look for: Seq Scan on large tables (needs index), high row estimates, sort operations
Join algorithms: Nested Loop (small tables), Hash Join (equality, medium), Merge Join (sorted, large)
Cost numbers are relative units - compare between query variations, not absolute values
Common optimizations: add missing indexes, rewrite subqueries as JOINs, limit data early
I regularly use EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL to optimize search queries in my NLP pipeline

question: What is database normalization? Explain 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF with examples.
hinglish_explanation: Normalization redundancy reduce karta hai data ko multiple tables mein split karke. 1NF: atomic values (no arrays in cells). 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency (all columns depend on full primary key). 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependency (non-key columns sirf key pe depend karein, doosre non-key pe nahi).
real_life_example: Zomato orders table: 1NF violation agar ek cell mein multiple items hain 'pizza,burger'. 2NF violation: composite key (order_id, item_id) mein customer_name sirf order_id pe depend karta hai. 3NF violation: city column hai aur state bhi - state city pe depend karta hai, directly primary key pe nahi.
how_to_answer: 1NF: atomic values in each cell, no repeating groups, unique rows with primary key
2NF: 1NF + no partial dependencies - every non-key column depends on ENTIRE composite key
3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependencies - non-key columns depend ONLY on primary key
BCNF: stronger 3NF - every determinant is a candidate key
Normalization reduces redundancy and update anomalies but increases JOINs needed
Denormalization: intentionally adding redundancy for read performance (common in analytics)
In ML systems: I denormalize for feature stores (fast reads) but normalize for transactional data

question: Explain different isolation levels in databases. What problems does each level solve?
hinglish_explanation: Isolation levels define karte hain ki ek transaction doosri concurrent transaction ka uncommitted data dekh sakti hai ya nahi. READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads allowed), READ COMMITTED (no dirty reads), REPEATABLE READ (no phantom reads mostly), SERIALIZABLE (fully isolated, slowest).
real_life_example: Banking app: READ UNCOMMITTED pe tu kisi ka transfer in-progress balance dekh sakta hai (wrong). READ COMMITTED pe sirf committed balance dikhega. REPEATABLE READ pe teri query ke beech koi balance change nahi dikhega. SERIALIZABLE pe sab sequential jaisa behave karega - safest but slowest.
how_to_answer: READ UNCOMMITTED: no locks, allows dirty reads - fastest but least safe, rarely used
READ COMMITTED: prevents dirty reads, but non-repeatable reads possible - PostgreSQL default
REPEATABLE READ: prevents dirty + non-repeatable reads, phantom reads possible in some DBs - MySQL InnoDB default
SERIALIZABLE: full isolation, appears sequential - prevents all anomalies but lowest concurrency
Dirty read: seeing uncommitted data that may be rolled back
Non-repeatable read: same query returns different values within same transaction
I use READ COMMITTED for most ML pipeline queries, SERIALIZABLE only for critical financial operations

question: How would you design a database schema for a high-throughput logging system that needs both fast writes and analytical queries?
hinglish_explanation: High-throughput logging mein write speed priority hai. Partitioning by time (daily/hourly), minimal indexes on write path, batch inserts, append-only tables. Analytics ke liye materialized views ya separate OLAP store (columnar). Basically OLTP aur OLAP concerns separate karo.
real_life_example: Flipkart event logging - har click, view, search log hota hai (millions per second). Write path: partitioned by date, minimal indexes, batch insert. Read/Analytics path: materialized views aggregate daily, ya data warehouse (Redshift/BigQuery) mein ETL. Dono same table se efficiently nahi ho sakta.
how_to_answer: Separate write-optimized (OLTP) and read-optimized (OLAP) paths - CQRS pattern
Write path: time-partitioned tables, minimal indexes, batch/bulk inserts, append-only
Partitioning strategy: range partition by timestamp - easy to archive/drop old partitions
Read path: materialized views for common aggregations, refreshed periodically
Consider columnar storage (TimescaleDB extension, or separate data warehouse) for analytics
Indexing: only essential indexes on write tables, comprehensive indexes on read replicas
In my work: ML inference logs partitioned by day, materialized views for model performance dashboards

question: How does Python's dictionary work internally? What is hash collision and how is it handled?
hinglish_explanation: Python dict hash table use karta hai. Key ka hash compute hota hai, phir modulo se index milta hai. Collision jab do keys ka same index aata hai - Python open addressing (probing) se handle karta hai, next available slot dhundhta hai. Python 3.7+ mein dicts insertion order maintain karte hain.
real_life_example: Library mein books ko rack number assign karna (hash function). Kabhi kabhi do books ko same rack aati hai (collision) - toh next available rack pe rakh dete hain (probing). Dictionary lookup O(1) average hai isliye ML mein feature lookup, caching, config storage sab dict mein hota hai.
how_to_answer: Python dict uses hash table: computes hash of key, maps to array index for O(1) average lookup
Hash collision: two keys map to same index - Python uses open addressing with probing
Load factor: when table is 2/3 full, it resizes (doubles) to maintain performance
Python 3.7+: dicts maintain insertion order - implemented with compact dict (split key/value arrays)
Keys must be hashable (immutable): str, int, tuple are valid; list, dict are not
__hash__ and __eq__ methods determine dict key behavior for custom objects
In ML: I use dicts for feature stores, embedding caches, config management - O(1) critical for serving

question: What are Python's collections module data structures? When would you use each?
hinglish_explanation: collections module specialized containers deta hai. defaultdict (missing key pe default value), Counter (counting), OrderedDict (ordered pre-3.7), deque (fast append/pop both ends), namedtuple (readable tuples). Ye built-in types se zyada efficient hain specific use cases ke liye.
real_life_example: Text analysis: Counter se word frequency count karo directly. deque se recent 100 API calls ka sliding window maintain karo. defaultdict(list) se documents ko category-wise group karo bina key existence check ke. namedtuple se database rows ko readable objects banao.
how_to_answer: defaultdict: auto-creates missing keys with default factory - no KeyError, cleaner code
Counter: specialized dict for counting - most_common(n), arithmetic operations on counts
deque: double-ended queue - O(1) append/pop from both ends, max length for sliding windows
namedtuple: immutable, memory-efficient alternative to class - accessed by name and index
OrderedDict: insertion order (pre-3.7), has move_to_end(), useful for LRU cache implementation
ChainMap: single view of multiple dicts - useful for layered configurations
I use Counter for token frequencies in NLP, deque for rate limiting, defaultdict for grouping embeddings

question: How does exception handling work in Python? Explain try-except-else-finally.
hinglish_explanation: try mein risky code daalo. except mein error handle karo. else tab chalta hai jab NO exception aaye (success path). finally HAMESHA chalta hai chahe error aaye ya na aaye (cleanup). Specific exceptions catch karo, bare except mat use karo.
real_life_example: ML model inference API: try mein model.predict() call karo. except ModelLoadError mein fallback model use karo. else mein result cache karo (success). finally mein GPU memory release karo chahe success ho ya failure. Production mein ye pattern robustness deta hai.
how_to_answer: try: contains code that might raise exceptions
except: handles specific exceptions - always catch specific types, not bare except
else: runs only when NO exception in try block - keeps success logic separate
finally: ALWAYS executes regardless of exception - cleanup (close connections, release resources)
Exception hierarchy: BaseException > Exception > specific exceptions (ValueError, TypeError etc)
Custom exceptions: inherit from Exception, add context for debugging
In production ML: I chain exceptions for traceability - raise CustomError() from original_error

question: How do you read and write files in Python? What are different file modes?
hinglish_explanation: Files open() function se open hoti hain. Modes: 'r' (read), 'w' (write, overwrite), 'a' (append), 'r+' (read+write), 'b' suffix binary ke liye. Hamesha 'with' statement use karo taaki file automatically close ho. Large files ke liye line by line read karo memory bachane ke liye.
real_life_example: ML pipeline mein: CSV training data 'r' mode mein read, model predictions 'w' mein write, logs 'a' (append) mein kyunki purana data preserve karna hai. Binary models (.pkl, .pt) 'rb'/'wb' mein. Bina 'with' ke file close bhool gaye toh data corrupt ho sakta hai.
how_to_answer: Always use 'with open()' context manager - ensures file is closed even on exceptions
Modes: 'r' (read), 'w' (write/overwrite), 'a' (append), 'x' (create, fail if exists)
Binary modes: 'rb', 'wb' for non-text files (images, pickled models, protobuf)
For large files: iterate line by line instead of read() to avoid memory issues
pathlib.Path is modern alternative: Path('file.txt').read_text() for simple reads
encoding='utf-8' always specify explicitly to avoid platform-dependent behavior
In ML: I use json/csv modules for data, pickle for models, and chunked reading for large datasets

question: Explain map, filter, and reduce in Python. When would you use them vs list comprehension?
hinglish_explanation: map() har element pe function apply karta hai. filter() condition ke basis pe elements filter karta hai. reduce() sab elements ko ek value mein combine karta hai (fold). List comprehension same kaam readable mein karta hai. map/filter lazy hain (iterator return karte hain), comprehension eager hai.
real_life_example: User reviews process karna: map(clean_text, reviews) - sab reviews clean. filter(lambda r: r.rating > 3, reviews) - positive reviews filter. reduce(lambda a,b: a+b.word_count, reviews, 0) - total word count. ML preprocessing mein ye functional style pipelines cleaner hoti hain.
how_to_answer: map(func, iterable): applies function to each element, returns iterator - lazy evaluation
filter(func, iterable): keeps elements where function returns True - lazy evaluation
reduce(func, iterable, initial): cumulatively applies function - imported from functools
List comprehension preferred for simple transformations - more Pythonic and readable
map/filter useful when: passing existing named functions, chaining operations, need lazy evaluation
reduce rarely used in modern Python - sum(), any(), all() replace common patterns
In ML pipelines: map for applying transforms to batches, filter for data quality checks

question: What are closures in Python? How are they related to decorators?
hinglish_explanation: Closure tab banta hai jab inner function outer function ki variables ko remember karta hai even after outer function return ho chuki hai. Variables encapsulated rehti hain. Decorators closures ka practical application hain - wrapper function original function ko remember karta hai closure mein.
real_life_example: Soch ek multiplier factory: make_multiplier(3) ek function return karta hai jo hamesha 3 se multiply karega. 3 closure mein saved hai. Decorator mein bhi same concept: timer decorator original function ko closure mein rakhta hai aur time measure karke call karta hai.
how_to_answer: Closure: inner function that captures and remembers variables from enclosing scope
Formed when: nested function references variable from outer function, outer function returns inner
The captured variables live on even after outer function has finished execution
Closures enable: function factories, data encapsulation, stateful functions without classes
Decorators are the most common practical application of closures in Python
nonlocal keyword: allows inner function to modify captured variable (not just read)
Use case in ML: creating configured preprocessing functions with embedded parameters

question: Write a SQL query to find the second highest salary from an Employee table.
hinglish_explanation: Classic interview question. Multiple approaches hain: subquery with MAX (second MAX excluding first MAX), LIMIT OFFSET (ORDER BY DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1), window function (DENSE_RANK), ya correlated subquery. Window function approach most flexible hai - Nth highest easily nikaal sakte ho.
real_life_example: HR analytics dashboard pe manager ko second highest paid employee dikhana hai department-wise. DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) use karega toh har department ka ranking mil jaayega - duplicates bhi handle ho jaayenge.
how_to_answer: Approach 1: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp)
Approach 2: SELECT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
Approach 3: WITH ranked AS (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) as rk) SELECT salary WHERE rk=2
DENSE_RANK handles ties correctly - if two people have highest salary, second highest is next distinct value
For Nth highest: change the rank filter to N - most generalizable approach
Edge cases to mention: NULL salaries, duplicate salaries, empty table
I prefer window function approach in production - readable, handles duplicates, generalizable

question: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP in SQL?
hinglish_explanation: DELETE rows remove karta hai with conditions (WHERE), logged hota hai, rollback ho sakta hai. TRUNCATE poori table khali karta hai (fast, minimal logging), auto-increment reset. DROP poori table structure hi delete kar deta hai - schema se gayab. DELETE DML hai, TRUNCATE/DROP DDL hain.
real_life_example: Flipkart database: DELETE FROM orders WHERE status='cancelled' - specific rows hatao (recoverable). TRUNCATE TABLE temp_analytics - test data jaldi clear karo (non-recoverable usually). DROP TABLE old_2020_logs - table hi nahi chahiye ab (gone forever).
how_to_answer: DELETE: removes specific rows (WHERE clause), fully logged, can be rolled back, triggers fire
TRUNCATE: removes ALL rows instantly, minimal logging, resets auto-increment, cannot use WHERE
DROP: removes entire table structure + data from database schema permanently
Performance: TRUNCATE >> DELETE for clearing tables - doesn't log individual row deletions
DELETE is DML (Data Manipulation), TRUNCATE and DROP are DDL (Data Definition)
TRUNCATE cannot be rolled back in most DBMS (MySQL), but can in PostgreSQL within transaction
Use cases: DELETE for selective cleanup, TRUNCATE for resetting staging tables, DROP for removing unused tables

question: Explain subqueries in SQL. What are correlated vs non-correlated subqueries?
hinglish_explanation: Subquery ek query ke andar doosri query hai. Non-correlated subquery independently execute hoti hai ek baar - result outer query use karti hai. Correlated subquery har outer row ke liye execute hoti hai (outer row reference karti hai) - slower but powerful. EXISTS typically correlated use karta hai.
real_life_example: Non-correlated: 'Sab employees jinki salary average se zyada hai' - average ek baar calculate hoga. Correlated: 'Har department mein highest salary wala employee' - har department ke liye subquery run hogi. Correlated slow hai lekin row-specific comparison ke liye zaruri hai.
how_to_answer: Non-correlated subquery: executes independently once, result used by outer query
Correlated subquery: references outer query columns, re-executes for each outer row
Non-correlated example: WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)
Correlated example: WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp e2 WHERE e2.dept = e1.dept)
EXISTS is typically correlated and often more efficient than IN for large datasets
Performance: non-correlated executes once, correlated can be O(n*m) without optimization
Modern optimizers often transform correlated subqueries to JOINs - check EXPLAIN plan

question: How do you write unit tests in Python? Explain pytest vs unittest and mocking.
hinglish_explanation: pytest simple hai - function likho test_ prefix ke saath, assert use karo, done. unittest Java-style class-based hai (setUp, tearDown). Mocking matlab fake objects bana ke external dependencies replace karna (API calls, DB). pytest fixtures dependency injection ka clean way hai.
real_life_example: ML model serving API test: actual model load nahi karna (slow), toh model.predict mock karo fixed output return karne ke liye. API endpoint test karo ki correct response format aa raha hai. Fixtures mein test data setup karo jo har test reuse kare.
how_to_answer: pytest: simpler syntax, powerful fixtures, parametrize decorator, better error messages
unittest: built-in, class-based (setUp/tearDown), familiar to Java/JUnit users
I prefer pytest: less boilerplate, fixture system, extensive plugin ecosystem
Mocking with unittest.mock.patch: replace external calls (APIs, DB, models) with controlled behavior
Fixtures: reusable test setup/teardown - @pytest.fixture with scope (function, module, session)
parametrize: run same test with different inputs - @pytest.mark.parametrize('input,expected', [...])
In ML: I mock model inference for unit tests, use integration tests for actual model behavior

question: Explain virtual environments in Python. What are venv, conda, and poetry?
hinglish_explanation: Virtual environment isolated Python environment hai - har project ke apne packages bina conflict ke. venv built-in lightweight hai. conda data science ke liye (non-Python deps bhi manage karta hai). poetry modern dependency management + packaging hai (lock file, build system).
real_life_example: Do ML projects: ek ko TensorFlow 2.10 chahiye, dusre ko 2.15. System-wide install mein conflict hoga. Virtual env se dono apne isolated space mein run karenge. Conda isliye popular hai data science mein kyunki CUDA toolkit bhi manage karta hai jo venv nahi kar sakta.
how_to_answer: Virtual env: isolated Python environment with own packages - prevents version conflicts between projects
venv: built-in (python -m venv), lightweight, pip-based - good for simple projects
conda: manages Python + non-Python deps (CUDA, C libraries), cross-platform - great for ML/data science
poetry: modern dependency resolver, lock files, build system, publishing - production-grade
pip-tools: pip-compile generates lock file from requirements.in - simpler than poetry
Docker: ultimate isolation for deployment - I containerize ML services with pinned dependencies
My workflow: conda for ML development (GPU deps), poetry for application packaging, Docker for deployment

question: How do you connect Python to databases? Compare raw SQL, ORMs (SQLAlchemy), and query builders.
hinglish_explanation: Python se DB connect karne ke multiple levels hain. Raw SQL (psycopg2/mysql-connector) - direct queries, full control. ORM (SQLAlchemy) - Python classes map to tables, object-oriented. Query builders - middle ground, programmatic query construction without full ORM overhead.
real_life_example: Mere Odoo project mein SQLAlchemy ORM use kiya models define karne ke liye. Complex analytics queries raw SQL mein likhe kyunki ORM se express karna mushkil tha. FastAPI app mein async SQLAlchemy use kiya non-blocking DB calls ke liye. Level of abstraction use-case pe depend karta hai.
how_to_answer: Raw SQL (psycopg2, mysql-connector): full control, best performance, but SQL injection risk without parameterization
ORM (SQLAlchemy, Django ORM): Python classes = tables, relationships managed, migrations support
Query builder (SQLAlchemy Core): programmatic SQL construction without full ORM overhead
Always use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection: cursor.execute('SELECT * WHERE id=%s', (id,))
Connection pooling (SQLAlchemy create_engine pool_size) essential for production performance
Async support: asyncpg for PostgreSQL, databases library for async ORM-lite queries
My approach: ORM for CRUD operations, raw SQL for complex analytics, async for high-concurrency serving

question: How do you handle database migrations in Python projects? Explain Alembic and migration strategies.
hinglish_explanation: Database migration matlab schema changes ko version control karna - jaise Git for database. Alembic (SQLAlchemy ke saath) migration scripts generate karta hai. Har change ek version hai - upgrade aur downgrade dono possible. Production mein zero-downtime migration strategies important hain.
real_life_example: Tera ML app mein user_queries table hai. Ab embeddings column add karna hai. Alembic se migration create karo, staging pe test karo, production pe apply karo. Agar kuch galat ho toh downgrade se revert. Bina migration tool ke production DB modify karna bahut risky hai.
how_to_answer: Alembic: migration tool for SQLAlchemy - generates version-controlled migration scripts
Auto-generate: alembic revision --autogenerate detects model changes vs current DB state
Each migration has upgrade() and downgrade() - reversible schema changes
Migration strategies: add column nullable first, backfill data, then add NOT NULL constraint
Zero-downtime: avoid locking operations on large tables - use concurrent index creation in PostgreSQL
Testing: run migrations on staging DB copy before production, include data migration tests
My workflow: model change → auto-generate → review migration → test on staging → apply to production

question: How do you optimize a slow SQL query in production? Walk through your debugging process.
hinglish_explanation: Pehle EXPLAIN ANALYZE run karo - dekho kahan time lag raha hai. Common fixes: missing indexes, full table scans, unnecessary subqueries, wrong join type. Statistics stale hain toh ANALYZE run karo. Partitioning, materialized views, query rewrite - sab tools hain optimization ke.
real_life_example: Mere search pipeline mein ek query 8 seconds le rahi thi. EXPLAIN se pata chala full table scan ho raha hai 5M rows pe. Composite index add kiya (user_id, created_at), query 50ms pe aa gayi. Phir frequently accessed results ko materialized view mein daala.
how_to_answer: Step 1: EXPLAIN ANALYZE to identify bottleneck - seq scans, high row estimates, sorts
Step 2: Check indexes - missing indexes on WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY columns, unused indexes
Step 3: Query rewrite - replace correlated subqueries with JOINs, use CTEs for clarity
Step 4: Statistics - run ANALYZE to update planner statistics if estimates are wrong
Step 5: Partitioning for large tables - partition by date/category for partition pruning
Step 6: Materialized views for expensive aggregations - refresh periodically
Real example: optimized NLP search query from 8s to 50ms using composite index + partial index on active records

question: How do you debug memory leaks in Python? What tools and techniques do you use?
hinglish_explanation: Memory leak jab objects deallocate nahi hote kyunki references retained hain unexpectedly. tracemalloc (built-in) memory allocation track karta hai. objgraph object references visualize karta hai. Common causes: circular references, global caches growing unbounded, closures retaining references.
real_life_example: ML serving API mein memory continuously badh rahi thi. tracemalloc se pata chala har request pe model output tensors cache mein accumulate ho rahe the bina eviction ke. LRU cache with maxsize add kiya aur memory stable ho gayi. Production mein ye common issue hai long-running services mein.
how_to_answer: tracemalloc: built-in, tracks memory allocations, shows top consumers and allocation source
objgraph: visualizes object reference graphs - find what's holding references to leaked objects
memory_profiler: line-by-line memory usage with @profile decorator
Common causes: unbounded caches, circular references, closures capturing large objects, global lists
gc.get_referrers(): find what's referencing a specific object preventing collection
weakref: use for caches that shouldn't prevent garbage collection
My debugging flow: monitor RSS over time → tracemalloc snapshot comparison → objgraph for reference chains

question: How do you implement a producer-consumer pattern in Python? Compare queue-based vs asyncio approaches.
hinglish_explanation: Producer-consumer: ek thread data produce karta hai, doosra consume. Queue shared buffer hai beech mein. threading.Queue thread-safe hai. asyncio.Queue async version hai. multiprocessing.Queue processes ke beech. Rate difference handle karta hai - slow consumer ke liye producer wait karega jab queue full ho.
real_life_example: ML pipeline: Producer thread documents read karta hai disk se. Consumer thread embeddings compute karta hai. Queue buffer hai - producer fast hai toh queue mein daal ke aage badhta hai, consumer apni speed se uthata hai. Mere RAG pipeline mein 3 producers (PDF parsers) aur 1 consumer (embedding model) aise connected hain.
how_to_answer: threading.Queue: thread-safe FIFO queue with put/get, blocking by default, maxsize for backpressure
asyncio.Queue: same interface but for coroutines - await queue.get() yields to event loop
multiprocessing.Queue: for inter-process communication - bypasses GIL for true parallelism
Backpressure: maxsize parameter - producer blocks when queue full, prevents memory overflow
Sentinel pattern: put None/STOP to signal consumers to shutdown gracefully
Multiple consumers: queue.task_done() + queue.join() for completion tracking
In my work: document ingestion pipeline with producer (file reader) → queue → consumer (embedding + indexing)

question: How do you implement soft deletes, audit trails, and temporal tables in SQL?
hinglish_explanation: Soft delete: row actually delete nahi karte, is_deleted=True ya deleted_at timestamp set karte hain. Audit trail: har change log hota hai (who, what, when). Temporal tables: row ka history maintain hota hai - kisi bhi past point pe data reconstruct kar sakte ho.
real_life_example: Banking app mein account delete nahi kar sakte compliance ke liye - soft delete use karte hain. Har transaction ka audit trail mandatory hai (RBI regulation). Temporal table se pata chal sakta hai ki customer ka address 3 mahine pehle kya tha - important for fraud investigation.
how_to_answer: Soft delete: is_deleted boolean or deleted_at timestamp - add WHERE deleted_at IS NULL to all queries
Implement via: application-level filter, database views, or row-level security policies
Audit trail: separate audit table logging old/new values, user, timestamp for every change
Triggers: database triggers auto-log changes - transparent to application code
Temporal tables: system-versioned tables (SQL:2011) - PostgreSQL temporal_tables extension
Pattern: effective_from, effective_to columns for manual temporal tracking (SCD Type 2)
In ML systems: I use soft deletes for training data (maintain reproducibility) and audit trails for model decisions

question: Explain Python type hints and type checking. How do you use typing module and mypy?
hinglish_explanation: Type hints Python mein optional annotations hain - runtime pe koi effect nahi lekin documentation aur tooling ke liye powerful. typing module se complex types (List[str], Dict[str, int], Optional, Union) define karte hain. mypy static type checker hai jo errors compile time pe catch karta hai.
real_life_example: ML API function: def predict(text: str, top_k: int = 5) -> List[Dict[str, float]]. Team ko immediately samajh aa jaata hai input/output kya hai. mypy se pata chal jaata hai ki kahi None return ho raha hai jahan List expected hai - production bugs prevent hoti hain.
how_to_answer: Type hints are optional annotations that don't affect runtime - PEP 484
Basic: def func(x: int, y: str) -> bool, variables: name: str = 'default'
typing module: List[T], Dict[K,V], Optional[T] (= Union[T, None]), Tuple, Callable
Python 3.10+: use | instead of Union, built-in generics (list[str] instead of List[str])
mypy: static type checker - catches type errors before runtime, integrates with CI/CD
TypedDict: type hints for dictionary structure - useful for API response typing
In my ML code: I type all function signatures for maintainability and use Protocol for duck typing

question: What are database locks? Explain optimistic vs pessimistic locking strategies.
hinglish_explanation: Locks concurrent access control karte hain. Pessimistic locking: pehle lock karo phir kaam karo (SELECT FOR UPDATE) - assume conflict hoga. Optimistic locking: kaam karo, save karte waqt check karo ki kisi ne change toh nahi kiya (version number) - assume conflict rare hai.
real_life_example: Movie ticket booking: Pessimistic - seat select karte hi lock (10 min timer, BookMyShow style). Optimistic - checkout pe check karo available hai ya nahi (conflict pe retry). High-contention (limited seats) mein pessimistic better, low-contention (wiki edit) mein optimistic.
how_to_answer: Pessimistic: acquire lock before reading/modifying - SELECT FOR UPDATE, prevents concurrent access
Optimistic: no locks during operation, check for conflicts at commit time using version/timestamp
Pessimistic use case: high contention scenarios (inventory, seat booking) - prevents lost updates
Optimistic use case: low contention (user profiles, content editing) - better concurrency
Optimistic implementation: version column, WHERE version=old_version on UPDATE, retry on conflict
Lock types: shared (read), exclusive (write), row-level, table-level, advisory locks
In my work: optimistic locking for ML model metadata updates, pessimistic for resource allocation

question: Explain the Singleton pattern in Python. What are different ways to implement it?
hinglish_explanation: Singleton matlab ek class ka sirf ek hi instance ho sakta hai poore program mein. Database connection, logger, config object - ye sab singleton candidates hain. Python mein module-level variable, __new__ override, metaclass, ya decorator se implement kar sakte ho.
real_life_example: ML model loading: 500MB model baar baar load nahi karna. Singleton pattern se pehli baar load hoga, baad mein same instance return hoga. Mere FastAPI app mein ModelManager singleton hai - har request pe naya model load nahi hota, shared instance use hota hai.
how_to_answer: Singleton ensures only one instance of a class exists throughout application lifecycle
Method 1: Module-level instance - Python modules are singletons by nature (imported once)
Method 2: __new__ override - check if instance exists, return existing or create new
Method 3: Metaclass - SingletonMeta controls class instantiation
Method 4: Decorator - wrap class to cache and return single instance
Thread safety: use threading.Lock in __new__ for concurrent access
In ML: I use singleton for model instances (expensive to load), connection pools, config objects

question: What is the Factory pattern in Python? How does it help in ML pipeline design?
hinglish_explanation: Factory pattern object creation logic ko centralize karta hai. Client ko exact class pata nahi hoti - factory decide karti hai kaunsa object banana hai based on input. ML mein useful hai jab different models, preprocessors load karne hain based on config without changing client code.
real_life_example: Mere pipeline mein ModelFactory.create('bert-base') ya ModelFactory.create('gpt-4') call karo - factory internally sahi class instantiate karegi (BERTModel, GPTModel). Client code same rahta hai chahe naya model type add ho. HuggingFace AutoModel.from_pretrained() exactly factory pattern hai.
how_to_answer: Factory pattern centralizes object creation logic - client doesn't need to know concrete classes
Simple Factory: function/method returns object based on parameter
Factory Method: subclasses decide which class to instantiate - template method for creation
Abstract Factory: family of related objects without specifying concrete classes
In Python: often implemented with dict mapping type_name → class, or __init_subclass__ registry
HuggingFace AutoModel is a real-world factory: AutoModel.from_pretrained() returns correct model class
My usage: ModelFactory in ML serving that creates correct model instance based on config/endpoint

question: What are f-strings in Python? How are they different from format() and % formatting?
hinglish_explanation: f-strings (Python 3.6+) sabse fast aur readable string formatting hai. f'Hello {name}' directly variable embed karta hai. % formatting purana C-style hai. .format() flexible hai lekin verbose. f-strings mein expressions bhi likh sakte ho: f'{x + y}', f'{obj.method()}'.
real_life_example: Logging ML metrics: f'Epoch {epoch}: loss={loss:.4f}, accuracy={acc:.2%}' - clean aur fast. Purane style mein 'Epoch %d: loss=%.4f' % (epoch, loss) likhna padta tha - hard to read. F-string mein debugging ke liye f'{variable=}' use karo - output: variable=42.
how_to_answer: f-strings (f'...'): inline expressions, fastest, most readable - Python 3.6+ preferred method
% formatting: C-style ('Hello %s' % name), legacy, limited - avoid in new code
.format(): 'Hello {}'.format(name), more flexible than %, but verbose compared to f-string
f-strings support: expressions f'{2+2}', method calls f'{s.upper()}', format specs f'{pi:.2f}'
Debugging: f'{variable=}' prints both name and value - Python 3.8+
Performance: f-strings fastest at runtime (compiled to efficient bytecode)
I use f-strings exclusively for logging, error messages, and query string construction in ML pipelines

question: Explain self-joins, anti-joins, and semi-joins in SQL. Give practical examples.
hinglish_explanation: Self-join: table khud se join hoti hai (employees and managers same table mein). Anti-join: wo rows jinke match NAHI milta doosri table mein (LEFT JOIN + WHERE IS NULL ya NOT EXISTS). Semi-join: rows jinke match EXISTS lekin sirf left table ke columns chahiye (EXISTS subquery).
real_life_example: Self-join: Employee table mein har employee ka manager name nikalo (manager bhi employee hai). Anti-join: Wo users jinke koi orders nahi (churned users for re-engagement campaign). Semi-join: Wo products jo kisi order mein hain (available products list).
how_to_answer: Self-join: table joined with itself using different aliases - hierarchical/comparative queries
Example: SELECT e.name, m.name as manager FROM emp e JOIN emp m ON e.manager_id = m.id
Anti-join: find rows with NO match - LEFT JOIN + WHERE right.id IS NULL or NOT EXISTS
Anti-join is often faster with NOT EXISTS than LEFT JOIN + IS NULL in some databases
Semi-join: check existence without returning matched columns - WHERE EXISTS (subquery)
Semi-join returns each left row at most once regardless of multiple matches in right table
Use cases in ML: self-join for computing user similarity, anti-join for finding unlabeled data

question: What is the iterator protocol in Python? How do you create custom iterators?
hinglish_explanation: Iterator protocol do methods hai: __iter__() (return self) aur __next__() (next value return karo ya StopIteration raise karo). Koi bhi object jo ye implement kare wo for loop mein use ho sakta hai. Generators automatically ye protocol implement karte hain.
real_life_example: Custom DataLoader banao jo batches yield kare: __iter__ har epoch pe data shuffle kare, __next__ next batch return kare. PyTorch DataLoader exactly aise kaam karta hai. Mere project mein custom iterator banaya tha jo PostgreSQL se paginated results fetch karta tha without loading all in memory.
how_to_answer: Iterator protocol: object implementing __iter__() (returns self) and __next__() (returns next value)
__next__ raises StopIteration when exhausted - signals end of iteration
Iterable vs Iterator: iterable has __iter__ returning iterator, iterator has both __iter__ and __next__
for loop internally calls iter() to get iterator, then next() repeatedly until StopIteration
Custom iterators useful for: database cursors, paginated API results, infinite sequences
Generators are syntactic sugar for iterators - less boilerplate with yield
In ML: custom iterators for streaming large datasets, batched processing, infinite data augmentation

question: What are common SQL string functions? Explain CONCAT, SUBSTRING, TRIM, REPLACE, and LIKE.
hinglish_explanation: String functions text manipulation ke liye hain. CONCAT strings jodta hai. SUBSTRING part nikalta hai. TRIM spaces hataata hai. REPLACE ek part ko doosre se replace karta hai. LIKE pattern matching ke liye hai (% = any chars, _ = single char).
real_life_example: User search pe: LIKE '%python%' se python mention wale courses milenge. Phone numbers clean karna: REPLACE(phone, '-', '') se dashes hata do. TRIM(name) se extra spaces hatao. CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) se full name banao display ke liye.
how_to_answer: CONCAT(str1, str2, ...): joins strings together - CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)
SUBSTRING(str, start, length): extracts portion - SUBSTRING(phone, 1, 3) for area code
TRIM(str): removes leading/trailing whitespace - LTRIM, RTRIM for specific sides
REPLACE(str, old, new): replaces all occurrences of substring
LIKE: pattern matching - % matches any characters, _ matches exactly one character
UPPER/LOWER: case conversion for case-insensitive comparisons
In my NLP pipeline: string functions for data cleaning before embedding generation

question: What are lambda functions in Python? When should and shouldn't you use them?
hinglish_explanation: Lambda ek anonymous (nameless) function hai jo ek expression evaluate karta hai. lambda x: x*2 matlab ek function jo input double kare. Chhoti operations ke liye useful jaise sort key, map/filter mein. Complex logic ke liye named function likho - lambda readable nahi rehta.
real_life_example: Sorting ML results by confidence: sorted(predictions, key=lambda p: p['score'], reverse=True). Pandas mein column transform: df['name'].apply(lambda x: x.strip().lower()). Lekin agar logic 2 lines se zyada hai toh proper function likho readability ke liye.
how_to_answer: Lambda: anonymous single-expression function - lambda args: expression
Use for: short operations as arguments to sort(), map(), filter(), reduce()
Cannot contain statements (if/else expression OK, but not if statement), assignments, or multiple expressions
Don't use when: logic is complex, needs documentation, or will be reused - use def instead
PEP 8: don't assign lambda to variable (lambda x: x*2) - use def instead for named functions
Common in pandas: df.apply(lambda x: ...), df.sort_values(key=lambda x: ...)
In ML code: I use lambdas for quick transformations in data pipelines and sort keys

question: Explain SQL aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. How do NULLs affect them?
hinglish_explanation: Aggregate functions multiple rows ko ek value mein combine karte hain. COUNT(*) sab rows count karta hai, COUNT(column) NULL skip karta hai. SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX sab NULL ignore karte hain. Ye GROUP BY ke saath use hote hain grouped results ke liye.
real_life_example: E-commerce analytics: COUNT(*) total orders, SUM(amount) total revenue, AVG(amount) average order value, MAX(amount) highest order. NULL handling important: agar 10 mein se 3 ratings NULL hain toh AVG sirf 7 ratings ka average lega, 10 ka nahi.
how_to_answer: COUNT(*): counts all rows including NULLs; COUNT(column): counts non-NULL values only
SUM/AVG: operate on non-NULL values only - NULLs are ignored, not treated as 0
MIN/MAX: return smallest/largest non-NULL value
COALESCE to handle NULLs: AVG(COALESCE(rating, 0)) treats NULL as 0
COUNT(DISTINCT column): counts unique non-NULL values
GROUP BY: aggregates apply per group, HAVING filters groups based on aggregate results
Gotcha: AVG with NULLs can be misleading - 3 values (5,5,NULL): AVG=5, not 3.33

question: How do you implement rate limiting for async API calls in Python? Explain semaphore and token bucket patterns.
hinglish_explanation: Rate limiting matlab API calls ko controlled speed pe karna taaki rate limits hit na ho. Semaphore concurrent calls limit karta hai (max 10 at a time). Token bucket time-based rate control hai - har second mein max N requests. asyncio.Semaphore aur custom token bucket common patterns hain.
real_life_example: OpenAI API rate limit: 60 requests/minute. Agar 1000 documents embed karne hain toh rate limiter lagana padega. Semaphore se max 5 concurrent calls. Token bucket se ensure karo ki per minute 60 se zyada na ho. Mere RAG pipeline mein exactly ye implement kiya hai.
how_to_answer: asyncio.Semaphore: limits concurrent operations - async with sem: await api_call()
Token bucket: tokens regenerate over time, each request consumes one - smooth rate limiting
Semaphore controls concurrency (how many at once), token bucket controls rate (how many per second)
Implementation: asyncio.Semaphore(10) for max 10 concurrent, custom class for token bucket
Exponential backoff: on 429 errors, wait 2^n seconds before retry - essential for production
aiohttp with semaphore pattern for batch API calls: gather tasks with semaphore-wrapped calls
My approach for LLM APIs: semaphore(5) + token bucket(60/min) + exponential backoff on rate limit errors

question: Explain database partitioning strategies. When would you use range, hash, or list partitioning?
hinglish_explanation: Partitioning large table ko smaller physical pieces mein todta hai for better performance. Range: value range se divide (date-wise). Hash: hash function se evenly distribute. List: specific values ke lists mein. Query optimizer sirf relevant partition scan karta hai (partition pruning).
real_life_example: Flipkart orders table: 500M rows. Range partition by order_date (monthly) - last month ke queries sirf ek partition scan karenge. Hash partition by user_id - even distribution across partitions for parallel queries. List partition by region (North, South, East, West) for region-specific analytics.
how_to_answer: Range partitioning: divide by value ranges - ideal for time-series data (date-based partitions)
Hash partitioning: distribute evenly using hash function - good for uniform distribution
List partitioning: explicit value lists per partition - good for categorical data (region, status)
Partition pruning: optimizer skips irrelevant partitions - dramatic performance improvement
Benefits: faster queries, easier maintenance (drop old partitions), parallel scanning
PostgreSQL: declarative partitioning with PARTITION BY RANGE/HASH/LIST
My use case: ML training logs partitioned by date - easy to archive old data, fast recent queries

question: How do you handle missing data in Pandas? What are strategies for NaN values in ML datasets?
hinglish_explanation: Pandas mein NaN missing data represent karta hai. dropna() rows/columns remove karta hai. fillna() se values fill kar sakte ho (mean, median, forward fill). ML mein strategy depend karta hai: numerical ke liye mean/median imputation, categorical ke liye mode ya 'missing' category, ya model-based imputation.
real_life_example: Customer churn dataset mein 20% income values missing hain. Drop karna data loss hai. Mean fill karna distribution change karta hai. Best approach: check if missing is random (MCAR) ya pattern hai. Mere project mein median imputation + missing indicator column add kiya tha feature engineering mein.
