real_life_example: Generator: data pipeline jo documents yield kare (producer). Coroutine: async function jo API call await kare (consumer/producer dono). Pehle @asyncio.coroutine + yield from likhna padta tha, ab async def + await - same concept, cleaner syntax.
how_to_answer: Generators: produce values with yield - for data streaming, lazy evaluation
Old-style coroutines: generators that receive values via .send() - PEP 342
yield from: delegate to sub-generator, foundation for old async - PEP 380
Native coroutines (3.5+): async def + await - dedicated syntax, not generator-based
Key difference: generators are iterators (pull), coroutines are for async control flow (cooperative)
Cannot yield from native coroutine, cannot await generator (different protocols)
Evolution: generator→generator coroutine→native coroutine - each step added clarity and performance

question: What are truthy and falsy values in Python? How does bool() conversion work?
hinglish_explanation: Python mein har object True ya False evaluate ho sakta hai. Falsy: None, False, 0, 0.0, '', [], {}, set(). Baaki sab Truthy hai. if statement mein direct object use kar sakte ho - if my_list: checks non-empty. Custom class mein __bool__ ya __len__ define karo truthy behavior ke liye.
real_life_example: if results: process(results) - agar results list empty hai toh skip, non-empty toh process. ML pipeline mein: if model: predict() - None model skip. if config.get('use_gpu'): use GPU. Ye Pythonic way hai explicit len(results) > 0 likhne se better.
how_to_answer: Falsy values: None, False, 0, 0.0, 0j, '', [], (), {}, set(), range(0)
Everything else is truthy - including non-empty collections, non-zero numbers, objects
bool(obj) calls __bool__() first, then __len__() if __bool__ not defined
Empty collections are falsy: if my_list: is Pythonic for checking non-empty
Custom class: define __bool__(self) to control truthiness - return True/False
Common pattern: result = value or default - uses truthiness for default values
In code: prefer if items: over if len(items) > 0: - more Pythonic and readable

question: How do you implement efficient pagination in SQL? Compare OFFSET vs cursor-based pagination.
hinglish_explanation: OFFSET pagination: LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20 - simple but slow for large offsets (skips N rows). Cursor pagination: WHERE id > last_seen_id LIMIT 10 - consistent O(1) performance. Large datasets pe OFFSET degrade hota hai kyunki database skip karne ke liye rows count karta hai.
real_life_example: API search results page 500: OFFSET 5000 matlab database 5000 rows skip karega (slow). Cursor: WHERE id > 4999 ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 - instant kyunki index direct seek karta hai. Infinite scroll apps (Instagram, Twitter) cursor pagination use karte hain.
how_to_answer: OFFSET: LIMIT n OFFSET m - simple but O(m+n) performance, degrades on deep pages
Cursor-based: WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n - O(n) always, consistent performance
OFFSET problems: slow on large offsets, inconsistent with concurrent inserts/deletes
Cursor advantages: consistent performance, stable results with concurrent modifications
Cursor limitations: can't jump to page N directly, only forward/backward navigation
Keyset pagination: cursor on composite keys - WHERE (created_at, id) > (:last_date, :last_id)
My APIs: cursor-based for user-facing pagination (infinite scroll), OFFSET only for admin/internal with small data

question: What is pyproject.toml? How has Python packaging evolved from setup.py?
hinglish_explanation: pyproject.toml modern Python packaging standard hai (PEP 517/518). setup.py purana way tha (executable, security risks). pyproject.toml declarative hai - metadata, dependencies, build system sab ek file mein. setuptools, poetry, flit sab pyproject.toml support karte hain.
real_life_example: ML library publish karna: pyproject.toml mein name, version, dependencies define karo. pip install . automatically build karega. Poetry: poetry init se pyproject.toml generate, poetry publish se PyPI pe upload. setup.py mein arbitrary code run ho sakta tha - security risk.
how_to_answer: pyproject.toml: PEP 517/518 standard - single file for project metadata, deps, build config
setup.py (legacy): Python script, arbitrary code execution during install - security concern
Evolution: setup.py → setup.cfg (declarative) → pyproject.toml (universal standard)
Build backends: setuptools, poetry-core, flit-core, hatchling - declared in [build-system]
Dependencies: [project.dependencies] for runtime, [project.optional-dependencies] for extras
Tools config: [tool.pytest.ini_options], [tool.mypy], [tool.ruff] - all in one file
My setup: pyproject.toml with setuptools backend, poetry for dependency management

question: What are LATERAL joins in SQL? When are they useful compared to regular joins?
hinglish_explanation: LATERAL join mein right side subquery left side ki current row refer kar sakti hai - basically correlated subquery but JOIN syntax mein. Har left row ke liye right subquery re-evaluate hoti hai. Top-N per group, dependent subqueries, set-returning functions ke liye useful.
real_life_example: Top 3 orders per customer: regular approach complex hai. LATERAL: SELECT u.*, o.* FROM users u, LATERAL (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = u.id ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 3) o. Har user ke liye top 3 orders directly - clean aur often faster than window function approach.
how_to_answer: LATERAL: subquery can reference columns from preceding FROM items - like correlated subquery in JOIN
Syntax: FROM table1, LATERAL (SELECT ... WHERE ref to table1 ...) AS subquery
Executes subquery for each row of left table - dependent/correlated evaluation
Use case 1: top-N per group - LATERAL with ORDER BY LIMIT per group row
Use case 2: set-returning functions applied per row - unnest, generate_series
Use case 3: complex dependent calculations that need outer row values
Performance: can be faster than equivalent window function + filter for top-N queries

question: How do you implement a parallel map-reduce pattern in Python for data processing?
hinglish_explanation: Map-reduce: data ko chunks mein split karo (map phase mein parallel process), results combine karo (reduce phase). multiprocessing.Pool.map() map phase handle karta hai. Results ko single thread mein reduce (combine) karo. Large dataset processing ke liye efficient parallel pattern.
real_life_example: 10M documents embed karna: map phase - 8 workers parallel mein chunks embed karein. Reduce phase - sab embeddings ek FAISS index mein combine. Pool.map(embed_batch, document_chunks) + results concatenate. Speedup ~7x on 8 cores (overhead se linear nahi hota).
how_to_answer: Map phase: split data into chunks, process each chunk in parallel worker
Reduce phase: combine results from all workers into final output
multiprocessing.Pool.map(func, chunks): parallel map with automatic chunk distribution
Pool.imap_unordered(): process results as they come - better for uneven workloads
chunk_size parameter: balance between overhead (too small) and load imbalance (too large)
Shared results: use Manager().list() or collect via return values and combine in main process
My pipeline: Pool(8).map(preprocess_chunk, text_chunks) for parallel preprocessing, reduce by concatenation

question: What is memoization? How is it different from caching? Implement a simple memoization decorator.
hinglish_explanation: Memoization specific optimization hai: function ke results store karo based on arguments - same args aayein toh stored result return karo without recomputing. Caching broader term hai (time-based, size-based, distributed). Memoization purely argument-based hai - pure functions pe kaam karta hai.
real_life_example: Fibonacci recursive: bina memoization O(2^n), with memoization O(n). ML mein: embedding function memoize karo - same text baar baar aaye toh API call skip. lru_cache(maxsize=1000) se top 1000 queries cached, baaki evicted.
how_to_answer: Memoization: cache function results keyed by arguments - avoids recomputation for same inputs
Only works for pure functions (same input → same output, no side effects)
functools.lru_cache: built-in memoization with LRU eviction - maxsize parameter
Implementation: dict mapping args tuple → result, check before computing
Difference from caching: memoization is argument-based, caching can be time-based/key-based
lru_cache limitations: args must be hashable, not suitable for methods (self reference)
In ML: memoize embedding calls, feature computations, expensive preprocessing steps

question: How do you convert rows to columns (pivot) and columns to rows (unpivot) in PostgreSQL?
hinglish_explanation: Pivot (rows→columns): CASE + GROUP BY ya crosstab() function. Unpivot (columns→rows): UNION ALL ya VALUES + LATERAL. PostgreSQL mein native PIVOT nahi hai (unlike SQL Server), toh CASE approach ya tablefunc extension ka crosstab() use hota hai.
real_life_example: Monthly report: data (product, month, sales) rows mein → pivot to columns (product, jan, feb, mar...). Crosstab(): SELECT * FROM crosstab('SELECT product, month, sales FROM data ORDER BY 1,2') AS ct(product text, jan int, feb int, mar int). Dynamic columns ke liye dynamic SQL zaruri.
how_to_answer: Pivot via CASE: SELECT grp, SUM(CASE WHEN cat='A' THEN val END) as A, ... GROUP BY grp
crosstab() (tablefunc extension): built-in pivot function - cleaner for known categories
Unpivot via UNION ALL: SELECT 'col1' as name, col1 as value UNION ALL SELECT 'col2', col2...
Unpivot via LATERAL: CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES ('col1', col1), ('col2', col2)) as t(name, val)
Dynamic pivot: use PL/pgSQL to generate query with dynamic column list
Limitation: SQL requires knowing columns at query write time - dynamic requires procedural code
Alternative: pivot in application layer (Pandas) when columns are dynamic

question: How do pytest fixtures work? Explain scope, parametrize, and conftest.py.
hinglish_explanation: Fixtures reusable test setup hai. @pytest.fixture se define karo, test function mein parameter name se inject hota hai. Scope: function (default, fresh per test), module, session. conftest.py mein shared fixtures rakh do - sab tests automatically access kar sakte hain. parametrize multiple inputs pe same test run karta hai.
real_life_example: ML testing: @pytest.fixture(scope='session') def model(): return load_model() - model ek baar load, sab tests share. @pytest.fixture def sample_text(): return 'Hello world'. conftest.py mein database fixture sab tests ke liye available. @parametrize se 10 different inputs pe same test.
how_to_answer: @pytest.fixture: defines reusable setup/teardown, injected by parameter name into tests
Scope: function (default, fresh each test), class, module, session (once per entire run)
yield fixture: code before yield is setup, after yield is teardown/cleanup
conftest.py: shared fixtures file - automatically discovered by pytest, no import needed
@pytest.mark.parametrize: run same test with multiple input/expected pairs
Fixture dependencies: fixtures can request other fixtures - dependency injection chain
My testing: session-scoped model fixtures, function-scoped DB (fresh state), parametrize for edge cases

question: How do you use conditional aggregation in SQL? Give examples of FILTER clause and CASE in aggregates.
hinglish_explanation: Conditional aggregation: ek GROUP BY mein multiple conditions ke aggregates nikalo. CASE inside SUM/COUNT ya PostgreSQL FILTER clause. Ek query mein multiple metrics nikaal sakte ho without multiple queries. Pivoting ka foundation bhi yehi hai.
real_life_example: E-commerce monthly report ek query mein: COUNT(*) as total_orders, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status='completed') as completed, SUM(amount) FILTER (WHERE status='completed') as revenue, AVG(amount) FILTER (WHERE city='Mumbai') as mumbai_avg. Multiple metrics ek scan mein.
how_to_answer: CASE in aggregate: SUM(CASE WHEN condition THEN value ELSE 0 END) - works in all databases
COUNT with CASE: COUNT(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 END) - counts conditional rows
FILTER clause (PostgreSQL): aggregate FILTER (WHERE condition) - cleaner syntax, same result
Multiple metrics in one query: avoids multiple passes over data, much more efficient
Example: SELECT month, SUM(CASE WHEN type='credit' THEN amount END) as credits, SUM(CASE WHEN type='debit' THEN amount END) as debits GROUP BY month
Combines with GROUP BY for multi-dimensional conditional metrics
In analytics: single query for dashboard metrics instead of separate queries per metric

question: How do you implement the observer pattern for event-driven systems in Python?
hinglish_explanation: Observer pattern: subject state change hone pe sab registered observers ko notify karta hai. Python mein: callback list maintain karo, event pe sab callbacks call karo. asyncio mein: async callbacks. Libraries: blinker, PyPubSub. Event-driven ML pipelines mein useful - model updated → retrain dependent models.
real_life_example: ML model registry: model deploy hone pe (event) → cache invalidate (observer 1) → monitoring alert (observer 2) → downstream models retrigger (observer 3). Sab independently register hain - new observer add karna matlab bas register karo, existing code change nahi.
how_to_answer: Observer: subject maintains list of observers, notifies all on state change
Python implementation: list of callback functions, subject calls each on event
Decoupling: subject doesn't know observer details, observers register/unregister dynamically
Async observer: await asyncio.gather(*[cb(event) for cb in callbacks]) for async notification
Libraries: blinker (Flask signals), PyPubSub, Python's built-in weakref for preventing leaks
Event-driven architecture: decouple components, add new handlers without modifying source
In ML: model registry events trigger cache refresh, monitoring, downstream pipeline execution

question: What are GROUPING SETS, CUBE, and ROLLUP in SQL? How do they enable multi-level aggregation?
hinglish_explanation: GROUPING SETS: multiple GROUP BY combinations ek query mein. ROLLUP: hierarchical aggregation (year→month→day + totals). CUBE: sab possible combinations ka aggregation. Instead of multiple queries UNION ALL, ek query mein sab levels ke aggregates mil jaate hain. Reporting ke liye powerful hai.
real_life_example: Sales report: city-wise total, month-wise total, grand total sab ek query mein chahiye. ROLLUP(city, month) dega: city+month detail, city subtotal, grand total. CUBE(city, month) har combination dega. BI dashboards mein drill-down reports aise bante hain.
how_to_answer: GROUPING SETS: explicitly define which grouping combinations you want - flexible
ROLLUP(a, b, c): hierarchical - (a,b,c), (a,b), (a), () - subtotals at each level
CUBE(a, b, c): all combinations - 2^n groupings including grand total
Equivalent to UNION ALL of multiple GROUP BY queries but in single pass - much faster
GROUPING() function: identifies which columns are aggregated (NULL means aggregated level)
Use case: summary reports with subtotals, cross-tabulation, hierarchical drill-down
In analytics: ROLLUP for time-based hierarchy (year/month/day), CUBE for multi-dimensional analysis

question: How do you efficiently process very large files in Python? What patterns work for 10GB+ files?
hinglish_explanation: Large files ke liye: line by line iterate karo (memory efficient), chunked reading (fixed size blocks), mmap (memory-mapped files for random access), multiprocessing for parallel chunk processing. NEVER read() entire file for large data - memory overflow hoga.
real_life_example: 10GB log file analyze karna: for line in open('huge.log') se line by line process (constant memory). CSV: pandas read_csv(chunksize=10000) se chunks mein. Binary: mmap se specific offsets read without loading full file. Mere pipeline mein: chunked processing + multiprocessing = 10GB in 5 minutes.
how_to_answer: Line-by-line: for line in open('file'): - constant memory, Python buffered reading
Chunked reading: file.read(8192) in loop - for binary or fixed-size processing
pandas chunks: pd.read_csv('large.csv', chunksize=10000) - process DataFrame chunks
mmap: memory-mapped file for random access without loading entire file
multiprocessing: split file into chunks (by byte offset), process in parallel
Generator pipeline: chain generators for multi-step processing without materializing
My approach: chunked pandas for structured data, line-by-line for logs, mmap for indexed binary files

question: What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE? When should you use each?
hinglish_explanation: EXPLAIN sirf plan dikhata hai (estimated costs, rows) - query execute NAHI karta. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually execute karta hai aur real timings + actual rows dikhata hai. ANALYZE slow queries pe use karo but destructive queries (DELETE, UPDATE) pe careful - actually execute hoga! EXPLAIN sufficient hai usually.
real_life_example: Slow SELECT pe: EXPLAIN ANALYZE run karo - actual vs estimated rows compare karo. Agar estimated 100 but actual 100000 toh statistics stale hain (run ANALYZE table). DELETE query pe: sirf EXPLAIN use karo, ANALYZE nahi (actually delete ho jaayega!) ya transaction mein wrap karo with ROLLBACK.
how_to_answer: EXPLAIN: shows estimated plan without executing - safe for any query, shows cost estimates
EXPLAIN ANALYZE: executes query and shows actual timings/rows - reveals estimation accuracy
Use EXPLAIN for: initial plan check, destructive queries (DELETE/UPDATE), production queries
Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE for: diagnosing slow queries, comparing estimated vs actual rows
Key insight: if estimated rows wildly different from actual → stale statistics, run ANALYZE table
EXPLAIN (BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON): additional detail about I/O and structured output
Safety: wrap EXPLAIN ANALYZE for DML in transaction: BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE...; ROLLBACK;

question: How do you implement a timeout decorator in Python? What about cross-cutting concerns?
hinglish_explanation: Timeout decorator: function ko maximum time deta hai execute karne ke liye - exceed hone pe exception raise. signal.alarm (Unix), threading.Timer, ya multiprocessing se implement. Cross-cutting concerns (logging, timing, auth, retry) decorators se cleanly separate hote hain core logic se.
real_life_example: ML model inference: @timeout(30) lagao predict function pe - agar 30 seconds mein response nahi toh TimeoutError, client ko 504 return. API calls: @timeout(10) @retry(3) chain karo. Cross-cutting: @log @time @authenticate @validate - sab concerns separate, composable.
how_to_answer: signal.alarm approach (Unix only): set alarm, raises in main thread after timeout
threading approach: run in thread, join with timeout, raise if not completed
multiprocessing approach: run in process, terminate after timeout - most reliable
Cross-cutting concerns: aspects that apply across many functions (logging, auth, caching, retry)
Decorators separate these concerns from core business logic - clean, composable, testable
Stack decorators for multiple concerns: @log @cache @retry @timeout - execution order matters
My production: timeout for ML inference (prevent hanging), retry for API calls, log for observability

question: What are database backup strategies? Explain logical vs physical backups and point-in-time recovery.
hinglish_explanation: Logical backup: SQL dump (pg_dump) - portable, slow for large DBs. Physical backup: file-system level copy (pg_basebackup) - fast, same version required. WAL archiving: continuous log shipping for point-in-time recovery. PITR: restore to any moment in time using base backup + WAL replay.
real_life_example: ML production DB: nightly pg_basebackup (full physical backup). WAL archiving to S3 continuous. Disaster pe: restore last base backup + replay WAL logs to 5 minutes before failure (PITR). Data accidentally deleted at 3pm → restore to 2:59pm. RTO < 30min, RPO < 5min.
how_to_answer: Logical (pg_dump): SQL statements, portable across versions, slow for large DBs, granular (table-level)
Physical (pg_basebackup): file-system copy, fast backup/restore, same PG version required
WAL archiving: continuous shipping of write-ahead logs - enables point-in-time recovery
PITR: restore base backup + replay WAL to specific timestamp - recover from any point
Strategy: daily full backup + continuous WAL archiving + tested restore procedures
RPO/RTO: Recovery Point Objective (data loss tolerance), Recovery Time Objective (downtime tolerance)
My setup: nightly pg_basebackup to S3, WAL archiving continuous, weekly restore tests

question: How do you implement graceful shutdown for async Python services? Explain signal handling.
hinglish_explanation: Graceful shutdown: SIGTERM/SIGINT receive hone pe naye requests band karo, existing requests complete hone do, cleanup karo (DB connections close, files flush), phir exit. asyncio mein signal handlers register karo jo shutdown flag set karein. Running tasks ko cancel ya complete hone do.
real_life_example: ML serving API: Kubernetes SIGTERM bhejta hai (pod terminating). Graceful shutdown: new requests reject, current inference complete hone do (max 30s), model unload, connections close, exit 0. Bina graceful shutdown ke: responses lost, data corrupted, clients get 502.
how_to_answer: Register signal handlers: loop.add_signal_handler(signal.SIGTERM, shutdown_handler)
Shutdown handler sets event/flag: shutdown_event.set() - signals all components to stop
Stop accepting new work: close server socket, reject new tasks
Wait for in-flight work: await asyncio.gather(*running_tasks) with timeout
Cleanup: close DB pools, flush buffers, release resources in finally blocks
Timeout: force-cancel remaining tasks after grace period (e.g., 30s for K8s)
My implementation: signal handler → stop accepting → drain queue → await tasks (30s timeout) → cleanup → exit

question: How do you ensure data integrity across multiple related tables? Explain transaction patterns.
hinglish_explanation: Data integrity matlab related data consistent rahe across tables. Transactions ensure atomicity - sab ya kuch nahi. SAVEPOINT partial rollback allow karta hai. Application-level checks + database constraints dono combine karo. Distributed transactions (2PC) multiple databases across ke liye.
real_life_example: ML experiment: experiment row + hyperparams rows + metrics rows sab ek transaction mein insert. Agar metrics insert fail ho toh sab rollback - partial experiment data nahi chahiye. SAVEPOINT se specific step retry kar sakte ho bina poora transaction rollback kiye.
how_to_answer: BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK: basic transaction boundary - all or nothing
SAVEPOINT: named point within transaction for partial rollback without losing all work
Database constraints: FK, CHECK, UNIQUE enforce integrity regardless of application bugs
Application-level: validate before writing, use transactions for multi-table operations
Idempotency: design operations to be safely retried - unique constraints + ON CONFLICT
Distributed: two-phase commit (2PC) for cross-database consistency - complex, avoid if possible
My approach: single-DB transactions for related writes, idempotent operations, constraints as safety net

question: What tools do you use for Python code quality? Explain linters, formatters, and type checkers.
hinglish_explanation: Code quality tools: Ruff (fast linter+formatter, replacing flake8+black+isort), mypy (type checking), pytest (testing). Pre-commit hooks se commit karne se pehle automatically check ho. CI/CD mein bhi run karo. Consistent code = less bugs, easier reviews, better collaboration.
real_life_example: Mere ML projects mein: Ruff format+lint on save. mypy strict mode catches type bugs before runtime. pre-commit hook sab check karta hai commit se pehle. CI mein: ruff check + mypy + pytest sab pass hona chahiye merge ke liye. Bugs 50% reduce hue type checking add karne ke baad.
how_to_answer: Ruff: ultra-fast linter + formatter (Rust-based) - replaces flake8, black, isort, pyupgrade
mypy: static type checker - catches type errors without running code, strict mode recommended
pytest: testing framework - fixtures, parametrize, plugins for coverage and more
pre-commit: git hooks that run checks before commit - fail-fast, consistent enforcement
CI integration: ruff + mypy + pytest in GitHub Actions - block merge on failure
Configuration: all in pyproject.toml - ruff, mypy, pytest settings in one place
My pipeline: Ruff (format+lint) → mypy (types) → pytest (tests) in pre-commit + CI

question: How do you build a production-ready database access layer in Python? Explain repository pattern and unit of work.
hinglish_explanation: Repository pattern: database access logic encapsulate karo classes mein (UserRepository, ModelRepository). Unit of Work: related operations ek transaction mein group karo. SQLAlchemy session Unit of Work implement karta hai. Clean architecture mein business logic database details se decouple hoti hai.
real_life_example: ML platform: ModelRepository.save(model), ExperimentRepository.get_by_id(id). Business logic sirf repository methods call kare - SQL directly nahi likhe. Unit of Work: experiment + metrics + artifacts sab ek session.commit() mein save. Testing mein InMemoryRepository inject karo - DB zarurat nahi.
how_to_answer: Repository pattern: encapsulates data access behind interface - UserRepo.get_by_id(), .create(), .list()
Unit of Work: groups related operations in single transaction - commit all or rollback all
SQLAlchemy Session: implements Unit of Work - tracks changes, commits atomically
Benefits: testable (mock repositories), swappable (change DB without business logic changes)
Dependency injection: pass repository to service layer - easy testing with fake implementations
async repositories: async def get_by_id() with asyncpg/async SQLAlchemy for non-blocking access
My architecture: Repository per entity, Service layer for business logic, SQLAlchemy sessions for UoW
